{{Short description|Expression which is not assigned an interpretation}} 
{{other uses|Undefined (disambiguation)}}

In mathematics, the term '''undefined''' refers to a [[Value (mathematics)|value]], [[Function (mathematics)|function]], or other [[Expression (mathematics)|expression]] that cannot be assigned a meaning within a specific [[formal system]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=What exactly does undefined mean? |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4524071/what-exactly-does-undefined-mean |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=en}}</ref> 

Attempting to assign or use an undefined value within a particular formal system, may produce [[Contradiction|contradictory]] or meaningless results within that system. In practice, mathematicians may use the term ''undefined'' to warn that a particular calculation or property can produce mathematically [[Consistency|inconsistent]] results, and therefore, it should be avoided.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Horvath |first1=Joan |title=Make: Calculus: build models to learn, visualize, and explore |last2=Cameron |first2=Rich |date=2022 |publisher=Make Community, LLC |isbn=978-1-68045-739-1 |edition=1st |series=Mathematics/Calculus |location=Santa Rosa, CA}}</ref>  Caution must be taken to avoid the use of such undefined values in a deduction or proof.

Whether a particular function or value is undefined, depends on the rules of the formal system in which it is used.  For example, the [[imaginary number]] <math>\sqrt{-1}</math> is undefined within the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of [[real number|real numbers]].  So it is meaningless to reason about the value, solely within the [[Domain of discourse|discourse]] of real numbers.  However, defining the imaginary number <math>i</math> to be equal to  <math>\sqrt{-1}</math>, allows there to be a [[Consistency|consistent]] set of mathematics referred to as the [[complex number]] plane.  Therefore, within the [[Domain of discourse|discourse]] of complex numbers, <math>\sqrt{-1}</math> is in fact defined.

Many new fields of mathematics have been created, by taking previously undefined functions and values, and assigning them new meanings.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Martínez |first=Alberto A. |title=Negative Math: How Mathematical Rules Can Be Positively Bent |date=2018 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-13391-1 |location=Princeton, NJ}}</ref>  Most mathematicians generally consider these innovations significant, to the extent that they are both internally [[Consistency|consistent]] and practically useful.  For example, [[Ramanujan summation]] may seem unintuitive, as it works upon [[divergent series]] that assign finite values to apparently infinite sums such as [[1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯]]. However, Ramanujan summation is useful for modelling a number of real-world phenomena, including the [[Casimir effect]] and [[bosonic string theory]].

A [[Function (mathematics)|function]] may be said to be undefined, outside of its [[Domain of a function|domain]].  As one example, <math display="inline">f(x)=\frac{1}{x}</math> is undefined when <math>x=0</math>.  As [[division by zero]] is undefined in [[algebra]], <math>x=0</math> is not part of the domain of <math>f(x)</math>.

== Other shades of meaning ==
In some mathematical contexts, undefined can refer to a [[primitive notion]] which is not defined in terms of simpler concepts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Definition:Undefined Term - ProofWiki |url=https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Definition:Undefined_Term |access-date=2024-12-03 |website=proofwiki.org}}</ref>  For example, in [[Euclid's Elements|Elements]], [[Euclid]] defines a point merely as "that of which there is no part", and a line merely as "length without breadth".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Euclides |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7HDWIOoBZUAC&pg=PA6 |title=Euclid's elements of geometry: the Greek text of J.L. Heiberg (1883 - 1885): from Euclidis Elementa, edidit et Latine interpretatus est I.L. Heiberg, in aedibus B.G. Teubneri, 1883-1885 |date=2008 |publisher= Lulu.com|isbn=978-0-615-17984-1 |editor-last=Fitzpatrick |editor-first=Richard |edition=2nd |location= |pages=6 |translator-last=Fitzpatrick |translator-first=Richard}}</ref> Although these terms are not further defined, Euclid uses them to construct more complex geometric concepts.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Waismann |first=Friedrich |title=Introduction to Mathematical Thinking: The Formation of Concepts in Modern Mathematics |publisher=Frederick Ungar Publishing Co. |year=1951 |isbn= |location=New York |pages=73 |translator-last=Benac |translator-first=Theodore J.}}</ref>

Contrast also the term ''[[undefined behavior]]'' in computer science, in which the term indicates that a function may produce or return ''any'' result, which may or may not be correct.

== Common examples of undefined expressions ==
Many fields of mathematics refer to various kinds of expressions as undefined. Therefore, the following examples of undefined expressions are not exhaustive.

=== Division by zero ===

In [[arithmetic]], and therefore [[algebra]], [[division by zero]] is undefined.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Euler |first=Leonhard |title=Elements of Algebra |publisher=Longman, Rees, Orme, & Co. |year=1770 |edition=4th |location=London |pages=28}}</ref>  Use of a division by zero in an arithmetical calculation or proof, can produce absurd or meaningless results.

Assuming that division by zero exists, can produce [[Consistency|inconsistent]] logical results, such as the following fallacious "proof" that one is equal to two<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Sultan |first1=Alan |title=The mathematics that every secondary school math teacher needs to know |last2=Artzt |first2=Alice F. |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-99413-2 |series=Studies in mathematical thinking and learning |location=New York |pages=6}}</ref>:{{Table alignment}}
{| class="defaultleft col1right"
|+Incorrect "proof" that <math>1=2 </math>
|<math>
x 
</math>
|<math>
= y 
</math>
|Define <math>
x 
</math> as equal to <math>
y 
</math>
|-
|<math>x^2 </math>
|<math>= xy </math>
|Multiply both sides of equation by <math>x </math>
|-
|<math>x^2 - y^2 </math>
|<math>= xy - y^2 </math>
|Subtract <math>y^2 </math> from both sides
|-
|<math>(x+y)(x-y) </math>
|<math>= y(x-y) </math>
|Factor both sides of equation
|-
|<math>x+y</math>
|<math>=y </math>
|Divide both sides of equation by <math>x-y</math>
|-
|<math>2y</math>
|<math>=y </math>
|Replace <math>x </math> with <math>y </math>, because we know that <math>x=y </math>
|-
|<math>2</math>
|<math>=1 </math>
|Divide both sides by <math>y </math>
|}
The above "proof" is not meaningful.  Since we know that <math>x=y</math>, if we divide both sides of the equation by <math>x-y</math>, we divide both sides of the equation by zero.  This operation is undefined in arithmetic, and therefore deductions based on division by zero can be contradictory.

If we assume that a non-zero answer <math>n</math> exists, when some number <math>k \mid k \neq 0</math> is divided by zero, then that would imply that <math>k = n \times 0</math>.  But there is no number, which when multiplied by zero, produces a number that is not zero.  Therefore, our assumption is incorrect.<ref name=":0" />

===Zero to the power of zero===
Depending on the particular context, mathematicians may refer to [[zero to the power of zero]] as undefined,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hafstrom |first=John Edward |title=Basic concepts in modern mathematics |date=1961 |publisher=Dover Publications, Inc |isbn=978-0-486-49729-7 |edition= |series=Dover books on mathematics |location=Mineola, New York |publication-date=2013 |pages=19}}</ref> indefinite,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Why is $0^0$ also known as indeterminate? |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1028244/why-is-00-also-known-as-indeterminate |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=en}}</ref> or equal to 1.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jena |first=Sisir Kumar |title=C programming: learn to code |date=2022 |publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC Press |isbn=978-1-032-03625-0 |edition=1st |location=Boca Raton, FL |pages=19}}</ref>  Controversy exists as to which definitions are mathematically rigorous, and under what conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is 0^0 |url=https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~alopez-o/math-faq/mathtext/node14.html |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=cs.uwaterloo.ca}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Zero to the zero power – is $0^0=1$? |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/11150/zero-to-the-zero-power-is-00-1 |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=en}}</ref>

===The square root of a negative number===
When restricted to the field of real numbers, the square root of a negative number is undefined, as no real number exists which, when squared, equals a negative number.  Mathematicians, including [[Gerolamo Cardano]], [[John Wallis]], [[Leonhard Euler]], and [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]], explored formal definitions for the square roots of negative numbers, giving rise to the field of [[complex analysis]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vaughan |first=Lena |date=April 1903 |title=A History of i = \sqrt 1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N-buAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA173 |journal=Mathematical Supplement of School Science |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=173–175 |via=Google Books}}</ref>

=== In trigonometry ===
In trigonometry, for all <math>n \in \mathbb{Z}</math>, the functions <math>\tan \theta</math> and <math>\sec \theta</math> are undefined for <math display="inline">\theta = \pi \left(n - \frac{1}{2}\right)</math>, while the functions <math>\cot \theta</math> and <math>\csc \theta</math> are undefined for all <math>\theta = \pi n</math>.  This is a consequence of the [[List of trigonometric identities|identities]] of these functions, which would imply a [[division by zero]] at those points.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=McCallum |first1=William G. |title=Calculus: Single and Multivariable |last2=Hughes-Hallet |first2=Deborah |last3=Gleason |first3=Andrew M. |date=October 2012 |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] |isbn=978-1-118-54785-4 |edition=6th |pages=40}}</ref>

Also, <math>\arcsin k</math> and <math>\arccos k</math> are both undefined when <math>k > 1</math> or <math>k<-1 </math>, because the range of the <math>\sin</math> and <math>\cos </math> functions is between <math>-1</math> and <math>1</math> inclusive.

=== In complex analysis ===
In [[complex analysis]], a point <math>z</math> on the [[complex plane]] where a [[holomorphic function]] is undefined, is called a [[Mathematical singularity|singularity]]. Some different types of singularities include:

* [[removable singularity|Removable singularities]] - in which the function can be extended holomorphically to <math>z</math>
* [[Pole (complex analysis)|Poles]] - in which the function can be extended [[meromorphic function|meromorphically]] to <math>z</math>
* [[essential singularity|Essential singularities]] - in which no meromorphic extension to <math>z</math> can exist

== Related terms ==

=== Indeterminate ===

The term ''undefined'' should be contrasted with the term ''[[Indeterminate form|indeterminate]]''.  In the first case, undefined generally indicates that a value or property can have ''no'' meaningful definition.  In the second case, indeterminate generally indicates that a value or property can have ''many'' meaningful definitions.  Additionally, it seems to be generally accepted that undefined values ''may not'' be safely used within a particular formal system, whereas indeterminate values ''might'' be, depending on the relevant rules of the particular formal system.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Davis |first1=Brent |title=The math teachers know: profound understanding of emergent mathematics |last2=Renert |first2=Moshe |date=2013 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-09779-0 |location=New York |pages=77–79}}</ref>

==See also==
*[[Analytic function]] - a function locally given by a convergent power series, which may be useful for dealing with otherwise undefined values
*[[L'Hôpital's rule]] - a method in calculus for evaluating indeterminate forms
*[[Indeterminate form]] - a mathematical expression for which many assignments exist
*[[NaN]] - the [[IEEE 754|IEEE-754]] expression indicating that the result of a calculation is not a number
*[[Primitive notion]] - a concept that is not defined in terms of previously defined concepts
*[[Singularity (mathematics)|Singularity]] - a point at which a mathematical function ceases to be well-behaved
